research.answer:
The question was matched to: smoke, smoke detection, iss. Below is what the indexed documents state about it, quoted with their sources.

**Evidence**
- SAME-R: The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke. [S1]
- SAME: The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke. [S2]
- SAME: Measurement of Smoke Particle Size under Low-Gravity Conditions; Properties of Smoke from Overheated Spacecraft Materials in Low-Gravity; Smoke Particle Sizes in Low-Gravity and Implications for Spacecraft Smoke Detector Design; Spacecraft Fire Detection: Smoke Properties and… [S3]
- DAFT / DAFT-2: Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter. DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. On the Moon, regolith dust will enter habitats: how will detectors discriminate dust from… [S4]
- SAME-R: Reflight of SAME: sizes of smoke particles produced by spacecraft materials (Kapton, silicone, lamp wick, Pyrell, Teflon) in low gravity, related to smoke generation and transport conditions, to evaluate spacecraft smoke detectors. [S5]
- Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter: DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. Limitation: Terrestrial test dust, not lunar regolith; feasibility test only. [S10]
- Detectors must be checked against microgravity smoke, not Earth smoke: SAME was designed around the hypothesis that, without buoyant flows, smoke particles from pyrolysing materials grow larger than in 1 g; SAME and SAME-R provide quantitative data on detector sensitivity to reduced-gravity smoke. Limitation:  [S11]

top_passage.text: The Saffire-II experiment was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire-I investigation, the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex. The Saffire-1I flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-II has a sample card that contains 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm.

top_passage.text: The Saffire-III experiments were performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire 1 investigation, the Saffire III investigation also used SIBAL as the sample material. However, the experiments were conducted at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s compared to 20 cm/s during Saffire I. The flow was either concurrent or opposed. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity.

top_passage.text: The BRE investigation hypothesizes that there can exist a regime of quasi-steady burning in microgravity as a function of materials properties. Steady burning may never be achieved, and only slowly changing unsteady flames are possible. The proposed tests aboard the ISS aims to query this hypothesis by establishing a range of quasi-steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in the microgravity environment. It is hypothesized that BRE can determine a range of burning conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point.

top_passage.text: OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.
